summary.text: Factoring each binomial coefficient into its lower-�scale counterpart and a product \(U(N,L)=\prod_{p\nmid i<L}(1+N/i)\), the proof uses a second-order expansion of \(U\) together with \(\sum i^{-2}\equiv0\pmod{p^t}\) and \(\sum i^{-1}\equiv0\pmod{p^{2t}}\), obtained respectively from the permutation \(i\mapsto2i\) and reflection, to control the product modulo \(p^{r+2t}\). Splitting the summation indices into multiples and nonmultiples of \(p\), these bounds make the former agree with \(p\) times the lower-level sum modulo \(p^{4r}\), while recursively merged inverse-square block sums cancel the latter modulo \(p^{4r}\); division by the outer factor loses \(r\) powers of \(p\), and separating the \(p\)-part of \(n\) gives the result.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
 a(N)=\frac1N\sum_{k=0}^{N}(N+2k)\binom{N+k-1}{k}^{3}
 \qquad(N\ge 1).
\]
We prove that for every prime \(p\ge5\), every \(n\ge1\), and every \(r\ge1\),
\[
 a(np^r)\equiv a(np^{r-1})\pmod {p^{3r}}.
\]

Throughout the proof, divisibility of rational numbers is understood \(p\)-adically: saying that a rational number \(q\) is divisible by \(p^e\) means \(v_p(q)\ge e\). Thus sums preserve the minimum of the divisibilities of their summands, products add divisibilities, and division by an integer prime to \(p\) does not change divisibility. Since \(p\ge5\), both \(2\) and \(3\) are units in this sense.

We first develop the reciprocal-sum and product estimates used later.

For \(i\ge0\), define
\[
 x_i=\begin{cases}
 0,&p\mid i,\\
 1/i,&p\nmid i.
 \end{cases}
\]
Also put
\[
 H_1(L)=\sum_{0\le i<L}x_i,
 \qquad
 H_2(L)=\sum_{0\le i<L}x_i^2,
\]
and, for a rational number \(N\),
\[
 U(N,L)=\prod_{0\le i<L}(1+Nx_i).
\]
Every \(x_i\), and hence every \(H_j(L)\), is \(p\)-integral.

### 1. A product expansion

Expanding the product \(U(N,L)\) through degree two gives
\[
 U(N,L)
 =1+NH_1(L)+\frac{N^2}{2}\bigl(H_1(L)^2-H_2(L)\bigr)+N^3R,
 \tag{1}
\]
where \(R\) is \(p\)-integral whenever \(N\) is \(p\)-integral.

Indeed, the coefficient of \(N\) is \(\sum_i x_i=H_1(L)\), while the coefficient of \(N^2\) is
\[
 \sum_{i<j}x_ix_j
 =\frac12\left(\left(\sum_i x_i\right)^2-\sum_i x_i^2\right).
\]
All terms of degree at least three can be collected as \(N^3R\); their coefficients are sums of products of the \(p\)-integral numbers \(x_i\), and \(2\) is a \(p\)-adic unit. Equivalently, (1) can be proved inductively by adjoining the last factor \(1+Nx_L\).

In particular, if \(v_p(N)\ge e\), then
\[
 U(N,L)\equiv1\pmod {p^e}.
 \tag{2}
\]
The same is true after taking cubes:
\[
 U(N,L)^3\equiv1\pmod {p^e},
 \tag{3}
\]
because \(X^3-1=(X-1)(X^2+X+1)\), and \(U(N,L)\) is \(p\)-integral.

### 2. A binomial-product identity

The main identity relating binomial coefficients at adjacent \(p\)-power levels is
\[
 \binom{pN'+L}{L}
 =\binom{N'+\lfloor L/p\rfloor}{\lfloor L/p\rfloor}
 U(pN',L+1).
 \tag{4}
\]

To prove it, induct on \(L\). It is immediate for \(L=0\), since \(x_0=0\). For the induction step, use
\[
 \binom{pN'+L+1}{L+1}
 =\binom{pN'+L}{L}\frac{pN'+L+1}{L+1}.
\]
If \(p\nmid L+1\), then \(\lfloor(L+1)/p\rfloor=\lfloor L/p\rfloor\), and
\[
 \frac{pN'+L+1}{L+1}=1+\frac{pN'}{L+1}=1+pN'x_{L+1},
\]
which supplies the new factor in \(U(pN',L+2)\). If \(p\mid L+1\), write \(L+1=pq\). Then \(x_{L+1}=0\), while the floor increases from \(q-1\) to \(q\); the usual recurrence for the smaller binomial coefficient gives exactly the ratio
\[
 \frac{N'+q}{q}=\frac{pN'+pq}{pq}.
\]
This proves (4).

Two consequences will be needed. If \(p\nmid k\), then
\[
 \binom{pN'+k-1}{k}
 =\frac{pN'}{k}
   \binom{N'+\lfloor k/p\rfloor}{\lfloor k/p\rfloor}
   U(pN',k).
 \tag{5}
\]
This follows by first writing
\[
 \binom{pN'+k-1}{k}
 =\frac{pN'}k\binom{pN'+k-1}{k-1}

a nd then applying (4) with \(L=k-1\); because \(p\nmid k\), one has \(\lfloor(k-1)/p\rfloor=\lfloor k/p\rfloor\).

If \(k'\ge1\), then
\[
 \binom{pN'+pk'-1}{pk'}
 =\binom{N'+k'-1}{k'}U(pN',pk').
 \tag{6}
\]
This is obtained similarly from (4), now with \(L=pk'-1\), followed by the elementary binomial recurrence.

### 3. Congruences for reciprocal sums

We next prove, for \(t\ge1\) and \(K\ge0\),
\[
 H_2(Kp^t)\equiv0\pmod {p^t},
 \tag{7}
\]
and
\[
 H_1(Kp^t)\equiv0\pmod {p^{2t}}.
 \tag{8}
\]

First consider (7) in the core case \(K=1\). Let \(M=p^t\). Multiplication by \(2\) is a permutation of the residue classes modulo \(M\), because \(2\) is coprime to \(M\). Thus the map
\[
 i\longmapsto 2i\bmod M
\]
permutes \(0,1,\ldots,M-1\). If \(p\mid i\), both \(x_i\) and \(x_{2i\bmod M}\) vanish. If \(p\nmid i\), then \(p\nmid 2i\bmod M\), and since
\[
 2i\bmod M\equiv2i\pmod {p^t},
\]
inversion of these \(p\)-adic units gives
\[
 x_{2i\bmod M}^2\equiv \frac14x_i^2\pmod {p^t}.

\]
Summing and reindexing by this permutation yields
\[
 H_2(M)\equiv\frac14H_2(M)\pmod {p^t}.
\]
Consequently \((3/4)H_2(M)\equiv0\pmod {p^t}\). Since both \(3\) and \(4\) are units modulo \(p\), this proves
\[
 H_2(p^t)\equiv0\pmod {p^t}.
\]

To pass to arbitrary \(K\), note that for every \(c,i\),
\[
 x_{cp^t+i}^2\equiv x_i^2\pmod {p^t}.
 \tag{9}
\]
If \(p\mid i\), both sides vanish. Otherwise \(cp^t+i\) and \(i\) are \(p\)-adic units differing by a multiple of \(p^t\), so their inverses, and then their squares, are congruent modulo \(p^t\). Splitting \([0,Kp^t)\) into \(K\) blocks of length \(p^t\), (9) shows that each block sum is congruent to the core block sum. This proves (7).

We now prove (8). Set \(L=Kp^t\), so \(p^t\mid L\), in particular \(p\mid L\). Reflection of the index set gives
\[
 H_1(L)=\sum_{0\le i<L}x_{L-i}.
 \tag{10}
\]
There is no endpoint problem here: \(x_0=x_L=0\). Adding (10) to the defining sum for \(H_1(L)\), and treating indices divisible by \(p\) as zero, gives
\[
 2H_1(L)
 =L\sum_{0\le i<L\atop p\nmid i}
       \frac1{i(L-i)}.
 \tag{11}
\]
For \(p\nmid i\), both \(i\) and \(L-i\) are units, and \(L-i\equiv-i\pmod {p^t}\). Therefore
\[
 \frac1{i(L-i)}\equiv-\frac1{i^2}\pmod {p^t}.
\]
The sum on the right side of (11) is thus congruent to \(-H_2(L)\), which is \(0\pmod {p^t}\) by (7). The outside factor \(L\) is itself divisible by \(p^t\), so (11) shows that \(2H_1(L)\) is divisible by \(p^{2t}\). Since \(2\) is a unit, (8) follows.

Combining (1), (7), and (8) gives a sharpened estimate for \(U\). If \(1\le t\le r\), \(p^t\mid L\), and \(N=mp^r\), then
\[
 U(N,L)\equiv1\pmod {p^{r+2t}}.
 \tag{12}
\]
Indeed, in (1), the linear term \(NH_1(L)\) has valuation at least \(r+2t\). The quadratic term has valuation at least \(2r+t\), because \(H_2(L)\) has valuation at least \(t\), while \(H_1(L)^2\) has even larger valuation; and \(2r+t\ge r+2t\) because \(r\ge t\). Finally the cubic remainder has valuation at least \(3r\ge r+2t\). By factoring a difference of cubes, (12) also implies
\[
 U(N,L)^3\equiv1\pmod {p^{r+2t}}.
 \tag{13}
\]

### 4. Block sums and an auxiliary weighted sum

For \(u\ge1\) and \(K\ge0\), define
\[
 \sigma_u(K)=\sum_{0\le i<p^u}x_{p^uK+i}^2.
\]
By (9) and the core case of (7),
\[
 \sigma_u(K)\equiv0\pmod {p^u}.
 \tag{14}
\]
Also, splitting a block of length \(p^{u+1}\) into \(p\) blocks of length \(p^u\) gives the exact merging identity
\[
 \sum_{K_2=0}^{p-1}\sigma_u(pK_1+K_2)=\sigma_{u+1}(K_1).
 \tag{15}
\]

For integers \(s,u,m,c\ge0\), with \(u\ge1\), define
\[
 \Omega_{s,u}(m,c)
 =\sum_{0\le K<cp^s}
   \binom{mp^s+K}{K}^{3}\sigma_u(K).
\]
We claim
\[
 \Omega_{s,u}(m,c)\equiv0\pmod {p^{s+u}}.
 \tag{16}
\]

We prove this by induction on \(s\). For \(s=0\), every binomial coefficient is an integer and every \(\sigma_u(K)\) is divisible by \(p^u\) by (14), proving the claim.

For the induction step, write each index at level \(s+1\) uniquely as
\[
 K=pK_1+K_2,
 \qquad 0\le K_1<cp^s,
 \quad 0\le K_2<p.
\]
Applying (4) gives
\[
 \binom{mp^{s+1}+pK_1+K_2}{pK_1+K_2}
 =\binom{mp^s+K_1}{K_1}
  U(mp^{s+1},pK_1+K_2+1).
 \tag{17}
\]
Replace the cube of the \(U\)-factor by \(1+(U^3-1)\). The contribution of \(1\), after summing over \(K_2\), is, by (15), precisely
\[
 \Omega_{s,u+1}(m,c),
\]
which is divisible by \(p^{s+u+1}\) by the induction hypothesis. In the remaining contribution, (2)--(3), applied to \(N=mp^{s+1}\), show that \(U^3-1\) is divisible by \(p^{s+1}\); meanwhile \(\sigma_u(pK_1+K_2)\) is divisible by \(p^u\) by (14). Hence every error summand is divisible by \(p^{s+u+1}\). This completes the induction and proves (16).

### 5. The summands at two adjacent levels

Define
\[
 \tau(N,k)=(N+2k)\binom{N+k-1}{k}^{3}.
\]
We first work in the case
\[
 N=mp^r,\qquad N'=mp^{r-1},\qquad p\nmid m,\qquad r\ge1,
\]
so that \(N=pN'\).

We split indices \(k\) according as \(p\mid k\) or not.

#### 5a. Indices divisible by \(p\)

Let \(k=pk'\), where \(k'\ge1\). By (6), if
\[
 C=\binom{N'+k'-1}{k'},
 \qquad
 U=U(N,pk'),
\]
then
\[
 \binom{N+pk'-1}{pk'}=CU.
\]
Since \(N+2pk'=p(N'+2k')\), it follows that
\[
 \tau(N,pk')-p\tau(N',k')
 =p(N'+2k')C^3(U^3-1).
 \tag{18}
\]
We show that the right side is divisible by \(p^{4r}\).

Write
\[
 k'=p^v k'',\qquad p\nmid k''.
\]
There are two cases.

First suppose
\[
 v+2\le r.
\]
Then \(p^{v+1}\mid pk'\), so (13), with \(t=v+1\), gives
\[
 v_p(U^3-1)\ge r+2(v+1).
 \tag{19}
\]
We also need the divisibility of \(C\). Put \(L=k'-1\). The elementary identity
\[
 \binom{N'+L}{L+1}
 =\binom{N'+L}{L}\frac{N'}{L+1}
\]
gives
\[
 C=\binom{N'+L}{L}\frac{N'}{k'}.
\]
The first factor is integral, and
\[
 \frac{N'}{k'}
 =\frac{mp^{r-1}}{p^vk''}
 =p^{r-1-v}\frac{m}{k''},
\]
where \(k''\) is a \(p\)-adic unit. Hence
\[
 v_p(C^3)\ge3(r-1-v).
 \tag{20}
\]
Moreover, both \(N'=mp^{r-1}\) and \(2k'=2p^vk''\) are divisible by \(p^v\), so
\[
 v_p(N'+2k')\ge v.
 \tag{21}
\]
Adding the contributions from (18)--(21), including the initial factor \(p\), gives
\[
 1+v+3(r-1-v)+r+2(v+1)=4r.
\]
Thus (18) is divisible by \(p^{4r}\) in this case.

Now suppose instead that \(v+2>r\), equivalently \(r\le v+1\). Then \(p^r\mid pk'\), so (13), now with \(t=r\), gives
\[
 v_p(U^3-1)\ge3r.
 \tag{22}
\]
Also \(r-1\le v\), so both \(N'\) and \(2k'\) are divisible by \(p^{r-1}\). Therefore
\[
 v_p\bigl(p(N'+2k')\bigr)\ge r.
 \tag{23}
\]
The integer \(C^3\) is \(p\)-integral. Equations (22) and (23) again show that (18) is divisible by \(p^{4r}\).

For \(k'=0\), the difference is exactly zero. We have therefore proved, for all \(k'\ge0\),
\[
 \tau(N,pk')-p\tau(N',k')\equiv0\pmod {p^{4r}}.
 \tag{24}
\]

#### 5b. Indices not divisible by \(p\)

Every nonmultiple of \(p\) in \([0,N]\) has a unique representation
\[
 k=pK+j,
 \qquad 0\le K<N',\quad 0\le j<p,\quad p\nmid j.
\]
For such \(k\), \(\lfloor k/p\rfloor=K\), and (5) gives
\[
 \binom{N+k-1}{k}
 =\frac Nk\binom{N'+K}{K}U(N,k).
 \tag{25}
\]
Write
\[
 C_K=\binom{N'+K}{K},\qquad U_k=U(N,k).
\]
Substituting (25) into \(\tau(N,k)\) and using \(N+2k\) gives
\[
 \tau(N,k)
 =N^4k^{-3}C_K^3U_k^3+2N^3k^{-2}C_K^3U_k^3.
\]
Separate from the second term its part with \(U_k^3\) replaced by \(1\):
\[
 \tau(N,k)=2N^3C_K^3k^{-2}+\rho(K,j),
 \tag{26}
\]
where
\[
 \rho(K,j)
 =N^4k^{-3}C_K^3U_k^3
 +2N^3C_K^3k^{-2}(U_k^3-1).
\]
Because \(p\nmid k\), all powers of \(k^{-1}\) are \(p\)-integral. The first term in \(\rho\) is divisible by \(N^4\), hence by \(p^{4r}\). For the second term, \(N^3\) supplies \(p^{3r}\), and (3) supplies another \(p^r\) in \(U_k^3-1\). Thus
\[
 \rho(K,j)\equiv0\pmod {p^{4r}}.
 \tag{27}
\]

It remains to sum the leading term in (26). For fixed \(K\),
\[
 \sum_{0\le j<p\atop p\nmid j}(pK+j)^{-2}=\sigma_1(K).
\]
Consequently
\[
 \sum_{K=0}^{N'-1}\sum_{0\le j<p\atop p\nmid j}
 2N^3C_K^3(pK+j)^{-2}
 =2N^3\Omega_{r-1,1}(m,m),
 \tag{28}
\]
because \(N'=mp^{r-1}\). By (16), \(\Omega_{r-1,1}(m,m)\) is divisible by \(p^r\). Since \(N^3\) is divisible by \(p^{3r}\), (28) is divisible by \(p^{4r}\). Combining this with (26)--(27) proves
\[
 \sum_{K=0}^{N'-1}\sum_{0\le j<p\atop p\nmid j}
 \tau(N,pK+j)
 \equiv0\pmod {p^{4r}}.
 \tag{29}
\]

### 6. Assembly and division by the index

The complete range \(0\le k\le pN'\) splits into the multiples \(pk'\), with \(0\le k'\le N'\), and the nonmultiples \(pK+j\) occurring in (29). Therefore (24) and (29) give
\[
 \sum_{k=0}^{pN'}\tau(pN',k)
 -p\sum_{k'=0}^{N'}\tau(N',k')
 \equiv0\pmod {p^{4r}}.
 \tag{30}
\]

We now relate these sums to \(a(N)\). First, the quotient defining \(a(N)\) is exact. Indeed, with
\[
 B=\binom{N+k-1}{N-1},
\]
the standard adjacent-binomial identity says
\[
 kB=N\binom{N+k-1}{N}.
\]
Thus
\[
 (N+2k)B^3
 =NB^3+2(kB)B^2
 =N\left(B^3+2\binom{N+k-1}{N}B^2\right),
\]
so each summand is divisible by \(N\). Also
\[
 \binom{N+k-1}{N-1}=\binom{N+k-1}{k}.
\]
It follows directly from the definition that
\[
 N a(N)=\sum_{k=0}^{N}\tau(N,k).
 \tag{31}
\]

Applying (31) at \(N=pN'=mp^r\) and at \(N'=mp^{r-1}\), the left side of (30) becomes
\[
 pN'a(pN')-pN'a(N')
 =mp^r\bigl(a(mp^r)-a(mp^{r-1})\bigr).

a
\]
Hence
\[
 mp^r\bigl(a(mp^r)-a(mp^{r-1})\bigr)
 \equiv0\pmod {p^{4r}}.
\]
Since \(p\nmid m\), division by the \(p\)-adic unit \(m\) and by \(p^r\) yields
\[
 a(mp^r)-a(mp^{r-1})\equiv0\pmod {p^{3r}}.
 \tag{32}
\]
Thus the desired supercongruence has been proved whenever the initial factor \(m\) is prime to \(p\).

### 7. Removal of powers of \(p\) already present in \(n\)

Finally, let arbitrary \(n\ge1\) be given. Write
\[
 n=p^j m,
 \qquad p\nmid m.
\]
Apply (32) with \(j+r\) in place of \(r\). Since \(j+r\ge1\), it gives
\[
 a(mp^{j+r})\equiv a(mp^{j+r-1})
 \pmod {p^{3(j+r)}}.
\]
But
\[
 mp^{j+r}=np^r,
 \qquad
 mp^{j+r-1}=np^{r-1}.
\]
Moreover, \(p^{3r}\mid p^{3(j+r)}\). Weakening the modulus therefore gives
\[
 a(np^r)\equiv a(np^{r-1})\pmod {p^{3r}},
\]
as required.
